title: Noetherian models of finite diagrams of split reductive groups
statement:
Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring. Let $I$ and $E$ be finite sets, with maps $s,t:E\to I$. For each $i\in I$ let $(G_i,T_i=D_A(M_i))$ be a split realization of a specified finite reduced root datum $(M_i,\Phi_i,M_i^\vee,\Phi_i^\vee)$ in [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization, def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group]. For each $e\in E$ fix an integer-lattice homomorphism $h_e:M_{t(e)}\to M_{s(e)}$ and a group-scheme homomorphism $f_e:G_{s(e)}\to G_{t(e)}$ whose restriction to the tori is $D_A(h_e)$. Fix $E'\subseteq E$, and assume each $f_e$ for $e\in E'$ is quasi-finite and surjective, meaning finite type with finite topological fibres and surjective on underlying spaces. Choose generators $X_{i,\alpha}$ of all root modules, for $i\in I$ and $\alpha\in\Phi_i$; these modules and differentials are the full-torus character modules and dual-number maps of [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Optionally prescribe any finite list of equalities between parallel finite composites of the $f_e$ and identity maps, and equalities between the differentials of such parallel composites on chosen $X_{i,\alpha}$, all of which hold over $A$.

There are a subring $A_0\subseteq A$ generated by finitely many elements as a ring, split realizations $(G_{i,0},T_{i,0}=D_{A_0}(M_i))$ of the same specified root data over $A_0$, root-module generators $X_{i,\alpha,0}$, and homomorphisms $f_{e,0}:G_{s(e),0}\to G_{t(e),0}$ restricting to $D_{A_0}(h_e)$, with isomorphisms $(G_{i,0},T_{i,0})\times_{A_0}A\simeq(G_i,T_i)$ identifying every $f_{e,0}$ and $X_{i,\alpha,0}$ with its specified counterpart. Every marked $f_{e,0}$, $e\in E'$, is quasi-finite and surjective, and every prescribed morphism and tangent-vector equality holds over $A_0$. In particular $A_0$ is a nonzero Noetherian ring [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. No reducedness or connectedness assumption on either ring is made; empty root sets and empty arrow sets are allowed.

source.place: Conrad, Reductive group schemes, Corollary 3.1.11 and proof, printed pp.88-89, and Lemma 3.2.5, pp.92-93; finite-presentation diagram descent and eventual equalities: Stacks limits.tex Tag 01ZM (lemma-descend-finite-presentation); marked arrows: Tags 07RR (lemma-descend-surjective) and 094M (lemma-descend-quasi-finite). The root-vector and fixed-datum refinements are a finite-data version of these results. Local Conrad PDF WANTED; read online. No SGA source is used.

proof.text: Index by the set $J$ of unital subrings $B\subseteq A$ generated by finitely many elements over $\mathbf Z$, ordered by inclusion. It is nonempty (the prime subring), directed (adjoin two finite generating lists), and its union is $A$ (adjoin any single element). Compatible ring maps from these subrings glue uniquely elementwise, so $A=\varinjlim_{B\in J}B$. Every $B$ is nonzero because its identity is that of $A$. Every ideal of $\mathbf Z$ is generated by its least positive element, or is zero; thus $\mathbf Z$ is Noetherian. Applying the finite-type Noetherian theorem to $\mathbf Z\to B$ makes every $B$ Noetherian. The affine-limit theorem identifies $\operatorname{Spec}A$ with $\varprojlim_J\operatorname{Spec}B$. All stages are affine, hence qcqs, and transition maps are affine. Restricting to subrings containing any fixed finite-type subring still gives the same union and limit.

source.place: Tags 01YW, 01YX; algebra.tex Tag 00FN; directed-union universal property written here

proof.text: For each $i$, apply framed reductive-pair descent with $\Psi=\Phi_i$ and the entire chosen list $(X_{i,\alpha})_{\alpha\in\Phi_i}$. Its hypotheses hold: the full-torus character condition is the conjugation coaction identity $\rho(X)=X\otimes e^\alpha$. Indeed evaluate this identity on every algebra point; conversely take the universal point in $D_A(M_i)(A[M_i])$ to recover the coaction identity. The root decomposition in the hypothesis gives exactly the required free framed decomposition including $\operatorname{Lie}(T_i)$. We obtain over some $B_i\in J$ a reductive pair with torus exactly $D_{B_i}(M_i)$, maximal on every geometric fibre, and all the specified root generators, coaction and decomposition. The conclusion identifies their scalar extensions with the given data over $A$. This is a model of one framed pair, not yet a model of the arrow diagram.

source.place: Corollary 3.1.11, pp.88-89; Section 4 introduction, pp.107-108; framed finite-data extraction stated in the cited node

proof.text: Check the specified coroots, which framed descent does not assert. The root-line theorem supplies the canonical coroot $c_{i,\alpha}:\mathbf G_{m,B_i}\to D_{B_i}(M_i)$ and says that it commutes with arbitrary base change. Over $A$ its base change is the canonical coroot of $(G_i,T_i)$, whose geometric fibres are the prescribed $\alpha^\vee$ by the split-realization definition; as both are Zariski locally constant functions $|\operatorname{Spec}A|\to M_i^\vee$ in the monomial classification of that theorem, it equals the monomial coroot $\alpha^\vee$ over $A$. For every $m\in M_i$, compare the pullbacks of $e^m$ along $c_{i,\alpha}$ and along the monomial map: these lie in $B_i[t,t^{-1}]$ and have equal images in $A[t,t^{-1}]$. The latter map is injective, coefficient by coefficient, since $B_i\subseteq A$. Their pullbacks therefore already agree over $B_i$, for every $m$. Thus the coroot is precisely the specified constant cocharacter, even on disconnected or nonreduced bases. The weight decomposition already gives exactly $\Phi_i$, so this pair is a split realization of the entire specified root datum.

source.place: Section 4 introduction and Theorem 4.2.6; Definition 5.1.1, p.136, especially its independent coroot condition (3); Laurent-coefficient injectivity argument supplied here

proof.text: Choose $B\in J$ containing every $B_i$ by adjoining the finitely many generating lists; if $I$ is empty take the prime subring. Pull the models to $B$. To apply the pinned base-change theorem choose a base $\Delta_i$ of $\Phi_i$: write $M_i\simeq\mathbf Z^r$ and put $f(x)=\sum_kN^{k}x_k$ with $N$ larger than twice every root coordinate, so $f(\alpha)\ne0$ for all $\alpha\in\Phi_i$. The root datum axioms give the perfect pairing, injective indexing and reflection permutations, so the crystallographic base theorem makes the indecomposable $f$-positive roots $\Delta_i$ linearly independent; induction on $f(\alpha)$ writes each $f$-positive root as a nonnegative sum of $\Delta_i$, and $-\alpha=s_\alpha(\alpha)\in\Phi_i$ covers the rest. Pin by $X_{i,\alpha}$, $\alpha\in\Delta_i$. The base-change theorem, with these auxiliary bases and pinnings forgotten afterwards, preserves their specified root data and all the root generators and identifies their scalar extensions with the given pairs over $A$. For each root, tensoring the isomorphism $B_i\simeq B_iX_{i,\alpha}$ gives $B\simeq BX_{i,\alpha}$, so generators of all root lines are preserved, not only those of the auxiliary pinning. In this application only its underlying split realization and the formula $\mathfrak g_{\alpha,B}=B\otimes_{B_i}\mathfrak g_{\alpha,B_i}$ are used; no compatibility with a chosen positive system is requested. Work henceforth over the tail $J_B$. Apply finite-family arrow descent to the given $f_e$ between these fixed models to obtain scheme morphisms $f_{e,C}$ at one $C\in J_B$. The source and target models are affine of finite presentation over $B$, as required. After each enlargement retain the scalar-extended models and their root vectors.

source.place: Tag 01ZM(2); split base change as in Conrad, Definitions 5.1.1 and 6.1.1 and the base-change use following Theorem 6.1.17

proof.text: Apply common-stage equality descent to the following finite list. For each arrow impose $f_e\mu_s=\mu_t(f_e\times f_e)$, $f_e1_s=1_t$ and $f_e\iota_s=\iota_t f_e$, and impose $f_e j_s=j_tD(h_e)$ on the torus inclusions. Add the prescribed equalities between parallel composites, with an empty composite the identity. All these hold over $A$. The domains used are the base scheme, the groups, their binary products and the split tori; all are affine of finite presentation. For products this follows from the tensor-product finite-presentation theorem; for the torus choose a lattice basis and use the finite Laurent presentation. Equality descent therefore makes every displayed identity hold at one later stage. The first three identities say exactly that every descended arrow is a group homomorphism; the fourth gives the prescribed torus restriction. Composition in a finite relation uses only its finitely many displayed arrows, even when the free path category is infinite.

source.place: Tag 01ZM(3); finite list of group-law, torus and diagram equations

proof.text: Each root generator at the current stage $C$ is, by the dual-number definition of the Lie module, a map $x_{i,\alpha}:\operatorname{Spec}C[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)\to G_{i,C}$ reducing to the identity. A prescribed tangent equality $d(u)(X_{i,\alpha})=d(v)(X_{i,\beta})$ between parallel composites is exactly the equality $u\circ x_{i,\alpha}=v\circ x_{i,\beta}$ of scheme morphisms. More generally use the stated input vectors on the two sides of each prescribed equality. The domain is affine finitely presented, with the single equation $\epsilon^2=0$; the target group is finitely presented. Apply equality descent to this finite list. This proves the tangent equalities at one stage using postcomposition on actual dual-number points, rather than assuming that a differential identity descends automatically. The scalar extension of $c(b)+\epsilon d(b)$ is $c(b)+\epsilon d(b)$ with coefficients mapped to the new base; hence these maps are exactly the retained root vectors at every enlargement.

source.place: Tag 01ZM(3), applied to dual-number morphisms; differential and root-vector conventions in the definition of the split realization

proof.text: The descended arrows are finitely presented as morphisms, not merely morphisms between finitely presented objects. To see this directly, let $R\to P,R\to Q$ be the coordinate presentations of its target and source, and let $P\to Q$ be the arrow. Write $P=R[y_1,\ldots,y_m]/J$, $Q=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(r_1,\ldots,r_l)$, and choose polynomials $q_j(x)$ representing the images of $y_j$. Then as a $P$-algebra $Q=P[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(r_1,\ldots,r_l,y_1-q_1,\ldots,y_m-q_m)$. Both inverse maps send $x_k$ to $x_k$ and $y_j$ to $q_j$; the relations $J$ already vanish in $Q$. This is a finite presentation of the relative arrow. In particular the locally-finite-presentation hypothesis for surjectivity descent and the finite-presentation hypothesis for affine quasi-finiteness descent hold.

source.place: Tag 00F4; explicit relative-presentation argument written here

proof.text: For each marked arrow write its coordinate map at the current stage $C$ as $P\to Q$. Over $D\in J_C$ put $P_D=D\otimes_C P$ and $Q_D=D\otimes_C Q$. The directed-subalgebra tensor-colimit theorem, identifies $\varinjlim_D P_D=A\otimes_C P$. For clarity the canonical cocone is colimiting: compatible maps $P_D\to U$ restrict to a single map $P\to U$ and compatible maps $D\to U$, which glue to $A\to U$; the tensor universal property gives the unique map $A\otimes_C P\to U$. Also $Q_D=P_D\otimes_P Q$ by the tensor pushout universal property. Thus affine quasi-finiteness descent applies over the target-ring system $(P_D)$ to the finitely presented $P$-algebra $Q$. Its limit morphism is the given quasi-finite $f_e$. Here the hypothesis written as finite type and finite topological fibres agrees with the quasi-finite notion by the finite-fibre criterion. Surjectivity descent applies to the same arrow over the qcqs base system $(\operatorname{Spec}D)$, using step 7 for local finite presentation. We obtain a stage for quasi-finiteness and one for surjectivity for each marked arrow.

source.place: Tags 094M (lemma-descend-quasi-finite), 07RR (lemma-descend-surjective); tensor-colimit identification as in algebra.tex Tag 033C

proof.text: Take a common upper bound $A_0\in J$ of these finitely many stages. Surjectivity is stable under arbitrary base change. Quasi-finiteness remains true because local quasi-finiteness and finite type are stable under base change; the source is affine and thus quasi-compact. The bounded-fibre theorem applied to this locally quasi-finite morphism with quasi-compact source gives finite fibres, and the finite-fibre criterion returns precisely the required quasi-finiteness. All equations persist by functoriality of scalar extension, and the split base-change theorem retains the root generators, the entire root datum, and the specified isomorphisms after extension to $A$. Step 1 gives that $A_0$ is nonzero and Noetherian. Empty lists impose no conditions: for $E=\varnothing$ there is no arrow descent, and if $I=\varnothing$ then $E=\varnothing$ and the prime subring suffices. For $\Phi_i=\varnothing$ the frame consists only of $\operatorname{Lie}(T_i)$ and the coroot and root-vector lists are empty.
